results.claim: For m,n≥2, the sortable component has Q=(mn)! states if m or n is even and Q=(mn)!/2 states if both are odd.
results.proof_sketch: A row push is an n-cycle and a column push is an m-cycle. Thus when m and n are odd every generator is even, so only even configurations are reachable. The sortable-instance characterization in the sealed source gives the converse and also says that if either dimension is even every permutation is reachable. Hence the component of the sorted state has exactly the stated size.

results.claim: On a p×q board where pushes in both directions are allowed, an involution π on any chosen row can be applied in at most 3q+3a₂(π) pushes, with the only side effect being a one-step cyclic shift, in a chosen direction, of the body of each of a₂(π) fixed auxiliary columns.
results.proof_sketch: Use the source's three-scan SwapPairs construction, assigning one distinct auxiliary column to each transposition. In its one-direction model, a required inverse column push is represented by p−1 forward pushes. In the bidirectional target model, replace that block by one opposite-direction push, which is exactly the same permutation. Each scan makes q row pushes and one push of every auxiliary column, hence 3q+3a₂(π) pushes. The source's position trace is unchanged: the requested pairs swap, every other chosen-row token stays fixed, each auxiliary-column body shifts by one, and all other positions remain fixed.

results.claim: Every even permutation is a product συ of two involutions with a₂(σ)=a₂(υ); every odd permutation is a product συτ where τ is a transposition and a₂(σ)=a₂(υ).
results.proof_sketch: Factor each cycle into two reflections. An odd-length cycle has factors containing equally many transpositions. An even-length cycle has two choices whose transposition counts differ by +1 or −1. An even permutation has an even number of even-length cycles, so alternate the two choices to balance the totals. For an odd permutation, leave one unit of imbalance and remove one transposition τ from the larger final involution. Combining the disjoint factors gives the stated products.

results.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FillColumns makes every column near-full using O(pq log q) pushes; the proof does not require p≤q.
results.proof_sketch: Each column is pushed at most p−1 times. Let Ψ count tokens lying in the body of a column other than their target column, and let f be the number of underfull columns. The conveyor argument shows that every complete block of q buffer-row pushes decreases Ψ by at least f/2. During a phase with q/2^i≤f<q/2^{i−1}, one has Ψ<(p−1)q/2^{i−1}, so fewer than 4p complete blocks occur. There are O(log q) phases, giving O(pq log q) row pushes, while all column pushes total O(pq). No inequality compares p with q.

results.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FloatMinimums transforms a matrix whose columns are all near-full into one whose columns are all body-full using O(pq) pushes.
results.proof_sketch: Near-fullness implies that the buffer row contains exactly one token for each target column. During one q-step sweep, each such token aligns with its target column. Rotate that column by at most p−1 steps until its unique target-buffer token is at the head, and never rotate it again during this procedure. Its body then contains exactly the p−1 nonbuffer tokens assigned to that column. The total is q+q(p−1)=pq.

results.claim: Given a p×q matrix in which every column is body-full, its buffer row can be sorted in O(q) bidirectional pushes while preserving the set of tokens in every column body.
results.proof_sketch: The heads are exactly the q buffer tokens. If their required permutation is even, factor it into two equal-size involutions and apply the bidirectional involution construction with opposite side-effect directions on the same auxiliary columns; every body shift cancels. If it is odd, use the corresponding factorization with one final transposition. That last call shifts one body cyclically but preserves its token set. Since every involution has at most q/2 transpositions, the total cost is O(q).

results.claim: For arbitrary m,n≥2 and N=mn, any m×n configuration can be transformed in O(N log m) pushes into one in which every row contains exactly its target-row token set. In particular, this costs O(N log min{m,n}) when m≤n.
results.proof_sketch: Transpose the board and relabel each target (r,c) as (c,r), obtaining dimensions p=n and q=m. Apply the dimension-independent FillColumns bound in O(pq log q), FloatMinimums in O(pq), and buffer-head cleanup in O(q). Every transposed column then contains its complete target-column token set. Transposing the description back gives correct target-row membership in the original board. Since pq=N and q=m, the cost is O(N log m). This proof is valid for tall boards too, but then its logarithm is log m, not log min{m,n}.

results.claim: The parent's short-dimension reorientation does not justify its former row-specific O(N log min{m,n}) conclusion on a fixed tall labeling.
results.proof_sketch: For the audited 3×2 input ((1,2),(3,5),(4,6)), that construction can output ((1,2),(5,4),(3,6)). The output columns are {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}, exactly their target-column sets, but its second and third rows are {4,5} and {3,6}, not the target-row sets {3,4} and {5,6}. Conceptually, orienting a tall board with its short dimension as rows exchanges the two coordinate objectives: oriented-row membership maps back to original-column membership. Thus the construction refutes the asserted transpose-back inference, although not the existential row-membership statement later recovered by a different argument.

results.claim: Assume 2≤m≤n and every row of a sortable m×n board already contains exactly its target-row token set. The board can then be sorted in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
results.proof_sketch: An even row correction is a product of two equal-size involutions; opposite-direction calls realize it in O(n) and cancel every off-row change. If a correction is odd and n is even, one row push makes the residual even. If n is odd and m is even, realize the even part and one transposition; the resulting cycle on an auxiliary column's m−1-cell body is even and can be reversed by two transposed involution calls in O(m). If both dimensions are odd, global sortability makes the number of odd row corrections even. Reduce each such row to the same adjacent transposition and pair the rows. Two four-push L-shaped commutators swap that adjacent pair in two adjacent rows; chaining them joins any row pair in O(m). The total is O(mn+m²)=O(mn).

results.claim: If min{m,n}=1 and N=mn, then D(m,n)=floor(N/2).
results.proof_sketch: Only the unique nontrivial row or column can move, so its reachable configurations are precisely its N cyclic shifts. A shift by a positions has distance d_N(a)=min(a mod N,N−(a mod N)); maximizing over a gives floor(N/2). This also covers N=1, where the diameter is zero.

results.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, and s=min{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·max{1,log s}); in particular, for m,n≥2, D(m,n)=O(N log s).
results.proof_sketch: For s≥2, orient the board as s×t with t=max{m,n}. Apply the row-membership construction with m=s, obtaining correct target-row sets in O(N log s), and then the row-sorting result in O(N). This use of transposition is legitimate because the entire sorting objective, unlike a row-specific intermediate conclusion on a fixed labeling, is coordinate-invariant. The one-dimensional result handles s=1.

results.claim: For all m,n≥2, including tall boards, every configuration can in fact be transformed in O(N log min{m,n}) pushes into one with correct target-row token sets, but this is a corollary of the diameter bound rather than of the refuted transpose-back construction.
results.proof_sketch: If either dimension is even, every configuration is sortable, so the diameter bound sorts it completely. If both dimensions are odd, the move group is A_N. An even configuration again sorts. For an odd configuration A, let B be the sorted board with two tokens in one row transposed. Then B is odd and has every target-row set correct. Since A and B have the same parity, their relative permutation is even; their Cayley-coset distance is therefore at most the identity-component diameter O(N log min{m,n}). Moving A to B proves the claim without circularity, because the diameter bound used only the short-row specialization of the earlier lemma.

results.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch: A row push changes the total cyclic horizontal displacement H by at most n and leaves V unchanged, so any sorting word contains at least ceil(H/n) row pushes. Symmetrically it contains at least ceil(V/m) column pushes, and the counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b). Rotating every row and column back along shortest directions attains the resulting lower bound.

results.claim: The maximum possible value of the displacement certificate is exactly m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2), which is at most N; a half-translation attains it.
results.proof_sketch: Each token contributes at most floor(n/2) to H and floor(m/2) to V. Hence H≤N floor(n/2) and V≤N floor(m/2), so ceil(H/n)+ceil(V/m)≤m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)≤N. Translating every token by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows makes every token attain both maxima simultaneously. Thus the bound is exact. Consequently, this entire displacement certificate is intrinsically only linear and cannot prove Ω(N log s) when s grows.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: The upper bound gives O(N log s)=O(N) for fixed s. A half-translation has exact distance m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2)=Ω(N), uniformly for dimensions at least two. Hence the bounds match. Together with the exact one-dimensional diameter, all fixed-short-side regimes have linear diameter.

results.claim: A general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: There are exactly Q sortable configurations. A geodesic word never immediately follows a generator with its inverse, so words of length at most L have at most 1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2) possible endpoints. Coincident generators on two-cell lines only make this an overcount. The radius-D ball must contain all Q states; rearranging that inequality gives the displayed ceiling.

results.claim: The numerical counting certificate above is always at most 2N, so this reduced-word obstruction also cannot establish a superlinear lower bound.
results.proof_sketch: Put X=1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d. Since Q>1, X<Q≤N!<N^N. Also d−1=2(m+n)−1>sqrt(N), using m+n≥2sqrt(N). Therefore log_{d−1}X<N log_{d−1}N<2N. Since 2N is an integer, ceil(log_{d−1}X)≤2N. Thus both quantitative lower-bound mechanisms retained here have an O(N) ceiling; closing the logarithmic gap requires a different metric obstruction or an improved upper bound.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: Exact breadth-first search with the seven distinct 2×3 generators visits all 720 configurations with level sizes [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], so the diameter is 7. The seven-push word R1-left, C1-up, R1-left, C1-up, C3-up, R1-right, C1-up reaches ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)), whose exact distance is 7. The displacement formula gives maximum translation distance 2·floor(3/2)+3·floor(2/2)=5.

results.claim: Exact square boundary cases give D(2,2)=4 and D(3,3)=8; on 3×3 the maximum displacement certificate is 6 and the counting certificate is 5.
results.proof_sketch: Complete BFS gives level sizes [1,4,10,8,1] on the 24-state 2×2 component and [1,12,96,736,5208,28674,89497,54741,2475] on the 181440-state 3×3 component. Thus their last nonempty levels are 4 and 8. The exact displacement maximum formula gives 4 and 6, while the reduced-word formula gives 2 and 5. Hence displacement is tight at 2×2 but already misses the diameter at 3×3; both quantitative certificates also miss at 2×3.

results.claim: For growing s=min{m,n}, the established general bounds remain Ω(N)≤D(m,n)≤O(N log s), so the source target is not resolved at its requested strength.
results.proof_sketch: Half-translations supply the uniform linear lower bound, and the short-row construction supplies the O(N log s) upper bound. The exact maxima above show only that the two available obstruction methods cannot produce the missing logarithmic factor; they do not prove that no different lower bound can. Conversely, no construction here removes the logarithm. Thus Θ(N) is proved for fixed s, but an unbounded gap remains when s grows.

final_writeup:
The audit correctly identifies a coordinate error in the parent's row-membership intermediate claim. Directly transposing an m×n board does establish target-row membership in O(mn log m) pushes. What fails for m>n is first reorienting the board so the short dimension is called the row dimension and then mapping a row-specific conclusion back: oriented rows become original columns. The audited 3×2 trace makes this concrete, producing correct column sets but incorrect row sets. Accordingly, that construction is retained only in its valid dimension-specific form.

This repair does not damage the diameter result. Let s=min{m,n}, t=max{m,n}, and N=mn. Orient the entire sorting problem as an s×t board and transpose it to t×s. The dimension-independent FillColumns potential argument makes every transposed column near-full in O(N log s) pushes. FloatMinimums makes the columns body-full in O(N), and bidirectional SwapPairs sorts the buffer heads in O(s) while preserving every body set. Mapping back now gives correct target-row membership on the deliberately chosen s×t orientation.

Those s rows can be sorted in O(N). Even row corrections are products of two equal-size involutions whose opposite body shifts cancel. Odd corrections are handled by a parity-changing row push when t is even, by repairing an even auxiliary-body cycle when s is even, or, on an odd-by-odd board, by pairing the necessarily even number of odd rows and using adjacent double-swap commutators. Hence D(m,n)=O(N log s) for s≥2; for s=1 the exact diameter is floor(N/2).

The original all-orientations row-membership statement can nevertheless be recovered after this diameter theorem, without the faulty transpose argument. If both dimensions are odd and the input permutation is odd, move it within its odd Cayley coset to the sorted board with one within-row transposition; that target is odd and already has correct row sets. All other configurations can be sorted completely. This yields O(N log s) row membership for every configuration, but only as a corollary, so the diameter proof is noncircular.

The obstruction/lower-bound lens exposes a precise limitation. The displacement certificate is maximized exactly by a half-translation and never exceeds m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)≤N. The reduced-word counting certificate never exceeds 2N: its logarithm is smaller than log_{d−1}(N^N)<2N because d−1>sqrt(N). Thus both sealed quantitative obstructions are intrinsically linear. Exact boundary enumeration gives D(2,2)=4, D(2,3)=7, and D(3,3)=8; translations or the two certificates already fail to be diametral on the latter boards.

Therefore the revision proves Θ(N) for every fixed short side and preserves the improved O(N log s) general upper bound, but it remains PARTIAL. When s grows, the bounds are still only Ω(N) and O(N log s). The obstruction analysis explains why the present lower-bound tools cannot close that gap; it does not establish that the logarithm is necessary.
